rv.q: Radcliffe lends himself beautifully to the material, while simultaneously allowing the crowd to curate the experience for themselves.
Radcliffe doesn’t just do away with the fourth wall, he manages to expand his magical aren’t-people-wonderful optimism to include the whole orchestra, mezzanine and balcony.
Instead, he twinkles through them, and his joy in the work is contagious.

Thanks in no small part to the radiant emotional authenticity Mr. Radcliffe brings to the role, the narrative of the protagonist’s life maintains our interest as he matures and himself begins to suffer from a persistent melancholy.
Clearly, everyone here understood all that what was really needed was Radcliffe and what he means to people.

What makes life worth living? For hard-core “Harry Potter” fans with money to burn, it might be getting Broadway tickets to interact fleetingly with Daniel Radcliffe in “Every Brilliant Thing,” an ingenious and touching solo performance piece written by Duncan Macmillan with Jonny Donahoe on the subject of suicide — or more precisely, on the ord...
It’s Radcliffe’s vitalizing and vulnerable performance, a cardio workout both physically and emotionally, that’s the reason to go.
The show works because Radcliffe more or less wills it to.
Primo tickets for Every Brilliant Thing cost more than $400, and if you don’t mind spending top dollar on a dime-thin show, this one won’t disappoint; it’s diverting and at times even touching.
We watch him, we watch him watch the dog die, and skeptics will be amazed to find within the very first minute that we believe every word of it.
Radcliffe has the audience in the palm of his hand.

The familiar music, touching premise, and Radcliffe’s winning personality combine to create an hour of theatre that, in spite of its subject of depression and suicide, manages in its life-affirming optimism to be both humorous and moving, while steering clear of undue schmaltziness.
It truly feels like we’re all at a party, celebrating life and all the little every day things that make it worth living.
For 70 minutes Radcliffe is arguably delivering the greatest male stage performance of the current New York theater season.
Any one-person show is obviously dependent on the magnetism of its performer, and Radcliffe is in total command of both the material and the room.
In fact, he’s the living definition of brilliant.

The principal storytelling fingerprints belong to writer Duncan Macmillan, a co-director of the current Broadway premiere with Jeremy Herrin, and to comedian Jonny Donahoe, who originally performed the show’s single interactive monologue in the United Kingd
Radcliffe is so affable a presence and so charming an interlocutor in each of his audience exchanges that the conceit works as well as it possibly can.
Mr. Radcliffe is a huge asset, of course: While I’ve never seen “Thing” in any of its previous incarnations, I can’t imagine a more charming, accessible player for these purposes.
I left delighted by the experience, albeit wishing the story had more substance.
What’s not lost is Radcliffe’s performance.
Even an actor of Radcliffe’s enormous charisma and charm can’t help but be buried in the deluge of audience participation that’s about to be unleashed.
How can we not root for Radcliffe as he delivers a tour de force, serotonin-boosting performance that’s as powerful as any drug currently on the market?

rv.q: A beautifully effective production that deserves to be added to the list of brilliant things.
The wondrous specificity of the brilliant things, the structure of the script, the palpable energy of the room, and the importance of the message make Every Brilliant Thing a visionary revolution.
His performance allows for humour without deflection and vulnerability without sentimentality.
And he pulls it off thanks to his inherent charm, wit, warmth as well as his ability to run swiftly while high fiving!
Daniel Radcliffe is everything you want in Every Brilliant Thing. Theatre just isn't the venue for it.
If you enter the theatre with a feeling that you already like Radcliffe, you will leave loving him.

cn.t: Radcliffe charms in this interactive solo show about depression and life's joys, with critics praising his warmth and audience engagement. Most find it touching if slight, though some question whether Broadway suits its intimate nature.
